stem.en: The coordination number of cobalt in [Co(en)₃]³⁺ is:

explanation.en: Ethane-1,2-diamine (en) is didentate: each of the three en ligands binds through two N atoms, so CN = 3 × 2 = 6.

stem.en: Which of the following is an ambidentate ligand?

explanation.en: NO₂⁻ can bind through N (nitrito-N) or through O (nitrito-O). NH₃ and H₂O have one donor atom; en has two donor atoms but binds through both.

stem.en: One mole of CoCl₃·5NH₃ is treated with excess AgNO₃ solution. The number of moles of AgCl precipitated is:

explanation.en: The compound is [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂: one Cl⁻ is bound to Co (secondary valence) and two are ionisable (primary valence), giving 2 AgCl.

stem.en: The oxidation number of nickel in [Ni(CO)₄] is:

explanation.en: CO is a neutral ligand and the complex is neutral, so Ni is 0.

solution.en: CO is a neutral ligand and the complex is neutral, so Ni is 0.

stem.en: Which of the following complexes will have the highest molar conductivity in aqueous solution (same concentration)?

explanation.en: [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃ gives 4 ions; the others give 3, 2 and 0 ions. More ions means higher molar conductivity.

stem.en: The IUPAC name of K₄[Fe(CN)₆] is:

explanation.en: In an anionic complex the metal name ends in -ate (ferrate for Fe). 4(+1) + x + 6(−1) = 0 gives Fe(II).

stem.en: The IUPAC name of [Cu(NH₃)₄]SO₄ is:

explanation.en: The complex is a cation, so the metal keeps its name: copper. SO₄²⁻ gives Cu(II).

stem.en: The formula of tris(ethane-1,2-diamine)cobalt(III) sulphate is:

explanation.en: [Co(en)₃]³⁺ and SO₄²⁻ combine 2 : 3 for neutrality: [Co(en)₃]₂(SO₄)₃.

stem.en: The IUPAC name of [Co(NH₃)₄(H₂O)Cl]Cl₂ is:

explanation.en: Ligands go in alphabetical order ignoring prefixes: ammine, aqua, chlorido. x − 1 = +2 gives Co(III).

solution.en: Ligands go in alphabetical order ignoring prefixes: ammine, aqua, chlorido. x − 1 = +2 gives Co(III).

stem.en: The IUPAC name of [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] is:

explanation.en: Neutral complex: metal keeps its name. Alphabetical order: ammine before chlorido. x + 0 − 2 = 0 gives Pt(II).

stem.en: [Co(NH₃)₅(SO₄)]Br and [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄ are examples of:

explanation.en: The ions inside and outside the coordination sphere are exchanged, so they give different ions in solution (Br⁻ vs SO₄²⁻).

stem.en: How many geometrical isomers does square planar [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] have?

explanation.en: MA₂B₂ square planar: cis (like ligands adjacent) and trans (opposite).

stem.en: Which complex can show linkage isomerism?

explanation.en: NO₂⁻ is ambidentate: it can bind through N (nitrito-N) or O (nitrito-O, the red isomer).

stem.en: The total number of stereoisomers of [CoCl₂(en)₂]⁺ is:

explanation.en: The trans isomer has a mirror plane and is optically inactive. The cis isomer is chiral and exists as d and l forms. Total = 1 + 2 = 3.

solution.en: The trans isomer has a mirror plane and is optically inactive.
The cis isomer is chiral and exists as d and l forms.

stem.en: Which of these shows optical isomerism?

explanation.en: [Co(en)₃]³⁺ has no plane of symmetry; its mirror images (d and l) cannot be superimposed. The others have mirror planes.

stem.en: The hybridisation of Ni in [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ is:

explanation.en: Ni²⁺ is 3d⁸. Strong-field CN⁻ pairs the electrons, freeing one 3d orbital: dsp², square planar, diamagnetic.

stem.en: [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ is:

options.en: an inner orbital complex and paramagnetic
an inner orbital complex and diamagnetic
an outer orbital complex and diamagnetic
an outer orbital complex and paramagnetic

explanation.en: Co³⁺ is 3d⁶. NH₃ pairs all six electrons into three 3d orbitals, leaving two 3d orbitals for d²sp³: inner orbital, no unpaired electrons.

stem.en: The geometry of [NiCl₄]²⁻ is:

explanation.en: Cl⁻ is a weak-field ligand; the two unpaired 3d electrons of Ni²⁺ stay unpaired and Ni uses sp³: tetrahedral and paramagnetic.

stem.en: The spin-only magnetic moment of [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ is:

explanation.en: Fe³⁺ is 3d⁵. CN⁻ forces pairing: t₂g⁵, one unpaired electron. μ = √3 = 1.73 BM.

solution.en: CN⁻ forces pairing: t₂g⁵, one unpaired electron. μ = √3 = 1.73 BM.

stem.en: Which of the following is diamagnetic?

explanation.en: In Ni(CO)₄, Ni(0) 3d⁸ 4s² rearranges to 3d¹⁰ and uses sp³: no unpaired electrons. The others have 2, 4 and 4 unpaired electrons.

stem.en: In an octahedral crystal field, the set of orbitals with higher energy is:

explanation.en: The lobes of d_x²−y² and d_z² point straight at the six ligands, so they are repelled more and rise by 0.6Δo.

stem.en: Which ligand produces the strongest crystal field?

explanation.en: Spectrochemical series: … Cl⁻ < … < H₂O < … < NH₃ < en < CN⁻ < CO. CO is the strongest.

stem.en: [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ is violet because:

options.en: it has a charge-transfer band in the infrared
its single 3d electron absorbs visible light in a d–d transition

explanation.en: Ti³⁺ (3d¹) absorbs blue-green light (about 498 nm) as the electron jumps from t₂g to e_g; we see the complementary violet colour.

stem.en: Ignoring pairing energy, the crystal field stabilisation energy of a low-spin d⁶ octahedral complex is:

explanation.en: Low spin d⁶ is t₂g⁶ e_g⁰: CFSE = 6 × (−0.4Δo) = −2.4Δo (plus pairing energy terms).

solution.en: Low spin d⁶ is t₂g⁶ e_g⁰: CFSE = 6 × (−0.4Δo) = −2.4Δo (plus pairing energy terms).

stem.en: Which of these complexes is high spin?

explanation.en: F⁻ is a weak-field ligand: Δo < P for Co³⁺, giving t₂g⁴ e_g² with 4 unpaired electrons. The other three are low-spin d⁶.

stem.en: The shape of [Fe(CO)₅] is:

explanation.en: Fe(CO)₅ is trigonal bipyramidal; Ni(CO)₄ is tetrahedral and Cr(CO)₆ octahedral.

stem.en: The metal–carbon bond in metal carbonyls has:

explanation.en: CO donates a lone pair to the metal (σ), and the metal donates d electrons back into the π* orbitals of CO (π back-bonding): synergic bonding.

stem.en: Which coordination compound is used to treat some kinds of cancer?

explanation.en: cis-Platin, cis-diamminedichloridoplatinum(II), inhibits the growth of tumours.

stem.en: The central metal ion in vitamin B₁₂ is:

explanation.en: Vitamin B₁₂ (cyanocobalamin) is a cobalt complex. Haemoglobin contains Fe and chlorophyll Mg.

solution.en: Vitamin B₁₂ (cyanocobalamin) is a cobalt complex.
Haemoglobin contains Fe and chlorophyll Mg.

stem.en: As π back-bonding from the metal to CO increases, the C–O bond:

options.en: becomes weaker and its stretching frequency falls
becomes stronger and its stretching frequency rises

explanation.en: Back-donation puts electrons into the π* orbitals of CO, lowering the C–O bond order. The M–C bond strengthens while the C–O bond weakens.

stem.en:
Assertion (A): [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ is diamagnetic.
Reason (R): CN⁻ is a strong field ligand; it pairs up the 3d electrons of Ni²⁺, giving dsp² hybridisation with no unpaired electron.

options.en: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation.en: Ni²⁺ is 3d⁸. With strong field CN⁻ the electrons pair into four 3d orbitals, one 3d orbital is used in dsp² (square planar), and no unpaired electron remains. R explains A.

stem.en:
Assertion (A): [CoF₆]³⁻ is a high-spin (outer orbital) complex.
Reason (R): F⁻ is a strong field ligand.

options.en: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation.en: F⁻ is a weak field ligand, so the 3d⁶ electrons of Co³⁺ stay unpaired (four unpaired electrons) and sp³d² hybridisation gives a high-spin complex. A is true; R is false.

passage.en: A purple solution of [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ is placed in a spectrophotometer, which shows maximum absorption at 498 nm (in the blue-green region). Ti³⁺ has a single 3d electron, so the absorption is due to one d–d transition from the t₂g to the e_g level. (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.)

stem.en: What is the crystal field splitting energy (Δₒ) of [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ in kJ mol⁻¹?

passage.en: A purple solution of [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ is placed in a spectrophotometer, which shows maximum absorption at 498 nm (in the blue-green region). Ti³⁺ has a single 3d electron, so the absorption is due to one d–d transition from the t₂g to the e_g level. (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.)

stem.en: If the water ligands were replaced by a stronger field ligand such as CN⁻, how would the absorption change?

options.en: It would shift to a longer wavelength because Δₒ decreases
It would shift to a shorter wavelength because Δₒ increases
It would not change because the metal ion is the same
The complex would stop absorbing because the d electron pairs up

explanation.en: A stronger field ligand increases Δₒ; a larger energy gap means light of higher energy, i.e. shorter wavelength, is absorbed.

stem.en: Which of the following show geometrical (cis–trans or fac–mer) isomerism? One or more options may be correct.

explanation.en: Square planar MA₂B₂ has cis and trans forms; octahedral MA₄B₂ has cis and trans; MA₃B₃ has fac and mer. [Co(en)₃]³⁺ (M(AA)₃) has no geometrical isomers; it shows only optical isomerism.

stem.en: Compare [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ and [FeF₆]³⁻. Which statements are correct? One or more options may be correct.

options.en: Both have the same spin-only magnetic moment

explanation.en: Fe³⁺ is 3d⁵. Strong-field CN⁻ pairs electrons: t₂g⁵, one unpaired, d²sp³ (inner orbital), μ = 1.73 BM. Weak-field F⁻ does not: five unpaired, sp³d² (outer orbital), μ = 5.92 BM. Both are octahedral, so the moments differ.

stem.en: [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ is a low-spin octahedral complex. Find the magnitude of its crystal field stabilisation energy in units of Δo, ignoring pairing energy (one decimal place).

explanation.en: Co³⁺ is d⁶; low spin gives t₂g⁶e_g⁰. CFSE = 6 × (−0.4Δo) + 0 × (0.6Δo) = −2.4Δo, so the magnitude is 2.4.

stem.en: Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment of [CoF₆]³⁻ in BM (two decimal places).

explanation.en: Co³⁺ is 3d⁶; F⁻ is a weak-field ligand, so the complex is high spin (t₂g⁴e_g²) with four unpaired electrons. μ = √(4 × 6) = √24 = 4.90 BM.

stem.en: The IUPAC name of K₃[Fe(C₂O₄)₃] is:

explanation.en: Oxalate is C₂O₄²⁻: x + 3(−2) = −3, so x = +3. The complex is an anion, so iron becomes "ferrate": potassium trioxalatoferrate(III).

solution.en: Oxalate is C₂O₄²⁻: x + 3(−2) = −3, so x = +3.
The complex is an anion, so iron becomes "ferrate": potassium trioxalatoferrate(III).

stem.en: One mole of CoCl₃·5NH₃ is treated with excess AgNO₃ solution. How many moles of AgCl are precipitated?

explanation.en: Coordination number 6: five NH₃ and one Cl⁻ are inside, [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂. Only the two outer chlorides are ionisable, giving 2 mol AgCl.

stem.en: The effective atomic number (EAN) of iron in [Fe(CO)₅] is:

explanation.en: Fe has Z = 26 and oxidation state 0; five CO donate 2 electrons each: EAN = 26 − 0 + 10 = 36, the electron count of krypton.

solution.en: Fe has Z = 26 and oxidation state 0; five CO donate 2 electrons each: EAN = 26 − 0 + 10 = 36, the electron count of krypton.

stem.en: The oxidation state of cobalt in [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂ is:

explanation.en: Two Cl⁻ outside means the complex ion is [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]²⁺. NH₃ is neutral, Cl is −1: $x - 1 = +2 \Rightarrow x = +3$.

stem.en: How many geometrical isomers does square-planar [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] have?

explanation.en: Two: cis (like ligands adjacent; this is the anticancer drug cisplatin) and trans (like ligands opposite). Tetrahedral MA₂B₂ would show none.

stem.en: The crystal field stabilisation energy of [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ (ignoring pairing energy) is:

explanation.en: Fe²⁺ is d⁶. CN⁻ is a strong-field ligand → low spin $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$. CFSE $= 6 \times (-0.4\Delta_o) = -2.4\Delta_o$. (High-spin d⁶ would give −0.4 Δo.)

stem.en: [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ is diamagnetic while [NiCl₄]²⁻ is paramagnetic. Their hybridisations are respectively:

explanation.en: Ni²⁺ is d⁸. Strong-field CN⁻ pairs up the electrons, freeing one 3d orbital → dsp², square planar, no unpaired electrons. Weak-field Cl⁻ leaves 2 unpaired electrons → sp³, tetrahedral.

stem.en: One mole of the complex CoCl₃·4NH₃, formulated as [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]Cl, is treated with excess AgNO₃. The moles of AgCl precipitated are:

explanation.en: Only chloride ions outside the coordination sphere (ionisable) precipitate with Ag⁺. Here one Cl⁻ is outside, so 1 mol AgCl forms.

stem.en: The total number of stereoisomers of the octahedral complex [Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺ is:

explanation.en: Geometrical: cis and trans. The trans isomer has a mirror plane and is optically inactive; the cis isomer is chiral and exists as a pair of enantiomers. Total $= 1 + 2 = 3$.

stem.en: The coordination number and the oxidation state of iron in K₃[Fe(CN)₆] are respectively:

explanation.en: Six CN⁻ ligands are bonded to Fe, so the coordination number is 6. Charge balance: $3(+1) + x + 6(-1) = 0$ gives $x = +3$. +2 is the value in K₄[Fe(CN)₆]; 3 is the number of K⁺ counter-ions, not ligands.

stem.en: One mole of CoCl₃·5NH₃ is treated with excess AgNO₃ solution at room temperature. How many moles of AgCl precipitate? (in mol)

explanation.en: Co(III) has a coordination number of 6. Five NH₃ and one Cl⁻ fill the inner sphere: [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂. Only the two ionisable (counter-ion) Cl⁻ react with Ag⁺, so 2 mol AgCl form. Answering 3 counts the coordinated chloride as well.

stem.en: The ethylenediaminetetraacetate ion (EDTA⁴⁻) is a:

explanation.en: EDTA⁴⁻ binds through two N atoms and four carboxylate O atoms, so it is hexadentate. Students often say tetradentate by counting only the four acetate groups and forgetting the two nitrogens.

stem.en: Which ligand forms a chelate ring with a metal ion?

explanation.en: A chelate forms when one ligand binds through two or more donor atoms, closing a ring with the metal. Ethane-1,2-diamine (en) binds through both N atoms and makes a five-membered ring. Cl⁻, H₂O and CO are monodentate.

stem.en: Which of the following is a homoleptic complex?

explanation.en: A homoleptic complex has only one kind of ligand. [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ has six NH₃ only. The other three contain two kinds of ligand (heteroleptic).

stem.en: In the spectrochemical series, which ligand produces the smallest crystal-field splitting?

explanation.en: The series runs I⁻ < Br⁻ < SCN⁻ < Cl⁻ < S²⁻ < F⁻ < OH⁻ < C₂O₄²⁻ < H₂O < NCS⁻ < edta⁴⁻ < NH₃ < en < CN⁻ < CO. Iodide is the weakest-field ligand; CN⁻ (and CO) are the strongest.

stem.en: Wilkinson's catalyst, used for the homogeneous hydrogenation of alkenes, is:

explanation.en: Wilkinson's catalyst is chloridotris(triphenylphosphine)rhodium(I), [RhCl(PPh₃)₃]. cis-[PtCl₂(NH₃)₂] is cisplatin (an anticancer drug), TiCl₄ + AlEt₃ is the Ziegler–Natta catalyst and [Ni(CO)₄] is the volatile carbonyl used in the Mond process.

stem.en: Match the biologically important compound with its central metal. (a) Chlorophyll (b) Haemoglobin (c) Vitamin B₁₂ (d) Cisplatin; (i) Co (ii) Pt (iii) Mg (iv) Fe

explanation.en: Chlorophyll is a magnesium complex, haemoglobin contains iron (haem), vitamin B₁₂ (cyanocobalamin) contains cobalt and cisplatin is a platinum(II) complex.

stem.en: For the same metal, ligands and metal–ligand distances, the tetrahedral splitting Δₜ is related to the octahedral splitting Δₒ by:

explanation.en: With only four ligands, none of which points straight at a d orbital, the splitting is smaller: $\Delta_t = \tfrac49\Delta_o$. Because Δₜ is usually smaller than the pairing energy, tetrahedral complexes are almost always high spin.

stem.en: According to Werner's theory, the secondary valence of the metal in a complex corresponds to its:

explanation.en: Werner's primary valence is ionisable and equals the oxidation state; it is satisfied by negative ions. The secondary valence is non-ionisable, equals the coordination number, is satisfied by neutral molecules or negative ions, and is directed in space, which gives the complex its definite geometry.

options.en: Oxidation state, satisfied by negative ions
Coordination number, satisfied by ligands and directed in space

stem.en: The hybridisation and magnetic behaviour of [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ are:

explanation.en: Ni²⁺ is $3d^8$. Strong-field CN⁻ pairs the eight electrons into four 3d orbitals, leaving one 3d orbital empty. That 3d with 4s and two 4p orbitals gives dsp² hybrids: square planar, no unpaired electrons, so diamagnetic. [NiCl₄]²⁻, with weak-field Cl⁻, is the sp³, paramagnetic case.

stem.en: Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment (in BM) of the tetrahedral complex [NiCl₄]²⁻. Give the answer to two decimal places. (in BM)

explanation.en: Ni²⁺ is d⁸. Weak-field Cl⁻ does not force pairing, so the complex is sp³ (tetrahedral) with 2 unpaired electrons (e⁴ t₂⁴ in crystal-field terms). $\mu = \sqrt{2(2+2)} = \sqrt8 \approx 2.83$ BM.

stem.en: Which of the following is an outer-orbital (high-spin) octahedral complex?

explanation.en: F⁻ is a weak-field ligand. In [CoF₆]³⁻ the six d electrons of Co³⁺ stay spread out (4 unpaired), so the inner 3d orbitals are not free and the complex uses sp³d² (4s, 4p, 4d) hybrids: outer orbital, high spin. NH₃ and CN⁻ pair the electrons, so the other three use d²sp³ (inner orbital).

stem.en: Ignoring pairing energy, the crystal-field stabilisation energy (CFSE) of a low-spin d⁶ octahedral complex is:

explanation.en: Low-spin d⁶ is $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$. CFSE $= 6(-0.4\Delta_o) + 0(+0.6\Delta_o) = -2.4\Delta_o$. The high-spin arrangement $t_{2g}^4 e_g^2$ would give $-1.6 + 1.2 = -0.4\Delta_o$.

stem.en: The CFSE of a high-spin d⁴ octahedral complex is $-x\,\Delta_o$ (ignoring pairing energy). Find $x$.

explanation.en: High spin d⁴: $t_{2g}^3 e_g^1$. CFSE $= 3(-0.4) + 1(+0.6) = -1.2 + 0.6 = -0.6\,\Delta_o$, so $x = 0.6$. The low-spin form $t_{2g}^4$ would give −1.6 Δₒ.

stem.en: The number of geometrical isomers of the octahedral complex [Co(NH₃)₃Cl₃] is:

explanation.en: An octahedral [MA₃B₃] complex has two geometrical isomers: fac (the three A on one triangular face) and mer (the three A in a plane passing through the metal, like a meridian). Neither is chiral.

stem.en: What is the total number of stereoisomers (geometrical + optical) of [Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺?

explanation.en: There are two geometrical isomers. trans-[Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺ has a mirror plane, so it is optically inactive. cis-[Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺ has no mirror plane and exists as a pair of enantiomers. Total $= 1 + 2 = 3$.

stem.en: Three hydrate isomers of CrCl₃·6H₂O are known. Which one gives 1 mol of AgCl per mole of complex with excess AgNO₃?

explanation.en: Precipitated AgCl equals the number of ionisable Cl⁻. [Cr(H₂O)₆]Cl₃ gives 3, [Cr(H₂O)₅Cl]Cl₂·H₂O gives 2 and [Cr(H₂O)₄Cl₂]Cl·2H₂O gives 1. [Cr(H₂O)₃Cl₃]·3H₂O would have no ionisable chloride and give 0.

stem.en: The violet colour of [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ is due to:

explanation.en: Ti³⁺ is d¹; in the octahedral field the electron sits in t₂g. It absorbs light (around 498 nm, blue-green) to jump to e_g. The colour seen is the complementary colour, violet. So the complex absorbs blue-green, not violet, light; e_g → t₂g would be emission, and charge transfer is not the cause here.

options.en: Transfer of an electron from H₂O to Ti³⁺
Promotion of an electron from e_g to t₂g
Promotion of the single d electron from t₂g to e_g

stem.en: Which order of ligand field strength is correct?

explanation.en: From the spectrochemical series: halides are weak, then O-donors (H₂O), then N-donors (NH₃, en), and C-donors (CN⁻, CO) are strongest. So Cl⁻ < H₂O < NH₃ < CN⁻.

stem.en: Compared with free carbon monoxide, the C–O bond in a metal carbonyl is:

explanation.en: Synergic bonding: CO donates its carbon lone pair to an empty metal orbital (σ bond) and the filled metal d orbitals donate back into the empty π* orbital of CO (π back-bond). Filling π* lowers the C–O bond order, so the C–O bond is longer and its stretching frequency is lower than in free CO.

options.en: Shorter, because CO donates its lone pair
Longer, because the metal back-donates electrons into the π* orbital of CO
Unchanged, because the bonding is purely σ
Shorter, because the metal removes electrons from π*

stem.en: The geometry and magnetic nature of [Ni(CO)₄] are:

explanation.en: Ni is in the 0 oxidation state ($3d^8 4s^2$). Strong-field CO pushes the 4s electrons into 3d, giving $3d^{10}$; the empty 4s and 4p orbitals form sp³ hybrids. So [Ni(CO)₄] is tetrahedral with all electrons paired (diamagnetic).

stem.en: The shape of iron pentacarbonyl, [Fe(CO)₅], is:

explanation.en: [Fe(CO)₅] has five CO ligands arranged trigonal bipyramidally around Fe(0) (dsp³). Octahedral is [Cr(CO)₆] and tetrahedral is [Ni(CO)₄]. Square pyramidal is the other five-coordinate shape, but it is not the one adopted by Fe(CO)₅.

stem.en: The stepwise formation constants for [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ have log K₁ = 4.0, log K₂ = 3.2, log K₃ = 2.7 and log K₄ = 2.0. What is log β₄, the overall formation constant? Give one decimal place.

explanation.en: $\beta_4 = K_1K_2K_3K_4$, so $\log\beta_4 = 4.0 + 3.2 + 2.7 + 2.0 = 11.9$. (Multiplying the log values, or averaging them, are common slips.) The steady fall from K₁ to K₄ is normal: each step has fewer water sites left to replace.

stem.en: The IUPAC name of [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl(NO₂)] (NO₂⁻ bonded through N) is:

explanation.en: Ligands go in alphabetical order of their names, ignoring 'di': ammine, chlorido, nitrito-N. The complex is neutral, so the metal keeps its normal name (platinum, not platinate). Oxidation state: $x + 0 - 1 - 1 = 0$, so $x = +2$.

stem.en: The correct formula of tetraamminediaquacobalt(III) chloride is:

explanation.en: Four NH₃ and two H₂O are neutral, so the cation carries the +3 charge of Co(III) and needs three Cl⁻: [Co(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]Cl₃. The Cl₂ option would mean Co(II); the last option swaps the counts of NH₃ and H₂O.

stem.en: Which aqueous solution (same concentration) has the highest molar conductivity?

explanation.en: Molar conductivity rises with the number of ions produced: [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃ gives 4 ions, [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂ gives 3, [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]Cl gives 2 and [Co(NH₃)₃Cl₃] gives none (non-electrolyte).

stem.en: Assertion (A): [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is paramagnetic, whereas [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ is diamagnetic. Reason (R): CN⁻ is a strong-field ligand and causes pairing of the d electrons of Fe²⁺.

explanation.en: Fe²⁺ is d⁶. With weak-field H₂O it is high spin ($t_{2g}^4 e_g^2$, 4 unpaired, paramagnetic). With strong-field CN⁻, Δₒ exceeds the pairing energy and all six electrons pair in t₂g ($t_{2g}^6$, diamagnetic). R explains A.

options.en: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

stem.en: How many geometrical isomers are possible for an octahedral complex of the type [Ma₂b₂c₂] (a, b, c are monodentate)?

explanation.en: Label each pair cis (C) or trans (T). Possible combinations: (T,T,T); (T,C,C), (C,T,C), (C,C,T) — one pair trans, other two cis; and (C,C,C) — all cis. (T,T,C)-type combinations are impossible, because if two pairs are trans the third must also be trans. Total geometrical isomers = 5. Only the all-cis isomer is chiral, so there are 6 stereoisomers in all.

stem.en: What is the total number of stereoisomers (including optical isomers) of [Co(en)(NH₃)₂Cl₂]⁺?

explanation.en: en occupies two cis sites. Of the remaining four, two are trans to the en donors and two are trans to each other (axial). (1) Both NH₃ axial (trans), both Cl trans to en: has a mirror plane. (2) Both Cl axial (trans): has a mirror plane. (3) NH₃ cis and Cl cis (one of each axial): no mirror plane, so it exists as two enantiomers. Total = 2 + 2 = 4 (three geometrical isomers).

stem.en: Which of the following statements is/are correct?

explanation.en: Co³⁺ is d⁶. NH₃ pairs the electrons ($t_{2g}^6$), freeing two 3d orbitals for d²sp³: inner orbital, diamagnetic (A). F⁻ is weak-field: 4 unpaired electrons remain, so sp³d² (outer orbital) is used (B), and $\mu = \sqrt{4 \times 6} = 4.90$ BM (D). C contradicts B.

options.en: [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ is an inner-orbital (d²sp³) complex and is diamagnetic
[CoF₆]³⁻ is an outer-orbital (sp³d²) complex with four unpaired electrons
The spin-only magnetic moment of [CoF₆]³⁻ is about 4.90 BM

stem.en: Which of the following species is/are optically active?

explanation.en: cis-[Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺ and [Co(en)₃]³⁺ lack any mirror plane or centre of symmetry and are chiral (Δ and Λ forms). trans-[Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺ has a mirror plane. Square planar cis-[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] lies in a plane, which is itself a mirror plane, so it is achiral.

stem.en: Which of the following statements about metal carbonyls is/are correct?

explanation.en: Synergic bonding gives the M–C bond σ (C → M) and π (M → CO π*) character (A). Back-donation into π* weakens the C–O bond, so B is wrong. [Cr(CO)₆] is octahedral (C). [Mn₂(CO)₁₀] is two square-pyramidal Mn(CO)₅ units joined by a Mn–Mn bond (D).

options.en: The M–C bond has both σ and π character
Back-donation from the metal strengthens the C–O bond

stem.en: Which of the following complexes is/are square planar?

explanation.en: [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ is dsp² square planar. Pt(II) (5d⁸) has a large Δ and is square planar even with Cl⁻. [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ is square planar (dsp² in VBT). [NiCl₄]²⁻ is tetrahedral (sp³) because Cl⁻ is weak-field.

stem.en: Which of the following octahedral complexes has zero CFSE?

explanation.en: High-spin d⁵ is $t_{2g}^3 e_g^2$: CFSE $= 3(-0.4) + 2(+0.6) = 0$. Low-spin [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ ($t_{2g}^5$) has −2.0 Δₒ, [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺ ($t_{2g}^3$) has −1.2 Δₒ and [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ ($t_{2g}^6$) has −2.4 Δₒ.

stem.en: [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ shows its d–d absorption maximum at 498 nm. Taking $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}$ J s, $c = 3.0 \times 10^8$ m s⁻¹ and $N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}$ mol⁻¹, Δₒ is about:

explanation.en: For d¹ the single band corresponds directly to Δₒ. $E = \dfrac{N_A h c}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.022\times10^{23} \times 6.626\times10^{-34} \times 3.0\times10^{8}}{498\times10^{-9}} \approx 2.40 \times 10^5$ J mol⁻¹ = 240 kJ mol⁻¹. Dividing by 2 or misplacing a power of ten gives the distractors.

stem.en: Which of the following neutral mononuclear carbonyls obeys the 18-electron rule?

explanation.en: Count metal valence electrons plus 2 per CO. Fe: 8 + 10 = 18. V: 5 + 12 = 17; Co: 9 + 8 = 17; Mn: 7 + 10 = 17. The 17-electron Co(CO)₄ and Mn(CO)₅ fragments reach 18 by dimerising (Co₂(CO)₈, Mn₂(CO)₁₀ with an M–M bond); V(CO)₆ is a rare stable 17-electron, paramagnetic carbonyl.

stem.en: Statement I: [Ni(NH₃)₆]²⁺ is an outer-orbital (sp³d²) complex. Statement II: Low-spin tetrahedral complexes are rarely observed because Δₜ is usually smaller than the pairing energy.

explanation.en: Ni²⁺ is d⁸: even with pairing, eight electrons fill four 3d orbitals and leave only one empty, but d²sp³ needs two. So the six-coordinate complex must use 4d orbitals (sp³d², 2 unpaired electrons): Statement I is correct. Δₜ = (4/9)Δₒ is nearly always below the pairing energy, so tetrahedral complexes are high spin: Statement II is correct.

options.en: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
